newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine beef exports seen held back by herd.
newsitem.headline: Argentine beef exports seen held back by herd.

text.p: Argentina's beef farmers have had good news and bad news this year, but industry chiefs fear that a falling stock of cattle may stop them fully taking advantage of their new official foot-and-mouth free status.

After a successful vaccination campaign and three years without an outbreak, Argentina was declared clean of foot-and-mouth disease in May. The United States swiftly granted final approval for a 20,000-tonne annual export quota of fresh beef, seen of great symbolic weight in persuading Japan and South Korea to open up their coveted markets.

But a tight domestic stock, caused by farmers being lured into arable farming by high grain prices and exacerbated by a long drought only just now ending, may make it hard for Argentina to export more beef.

"I calculate that exports will be a bit less than last year, or more or less the same," Estela Martinez, manager of the Argentine Beef Industry Association, told Reuters. "Although some new export possibilities have presented themselves, we are a bit worried about the supply of cattle."
She said that Argentina's herd had fallen to 51 million head in 1996 from 53.2 million head in 1994, and that the process seemed to be continuing.

Beef exports in the first five months of the year fell 5.3 percent in comparison with the same period in 1996 to 181,000 tonnes, carcass weight, according to Alberto de las Carreras, a former Argentine Trade Secretary and a director of the International Meat Secretariat.
"There is a very big factor, which is the bad shape of the European market after the "mad cow" scare," de las Carreras said. "That looks like lingering a bit."
He agreed that while new sales opportunities were appearing, tight stock might make it hard for exports to pick up much in the second half of the year.

Russia approved imports of Argentine beef earlier this year, and Cordoba province packers Col Car and Frigorifico Novara said Tuesday that they had signed an agreement to export 29,200 tonnes of beef a year to a private buyer supplying the Russian army through the year 2000.
The government says that it hopes beef exports will hit a million tonnes a year by 2000, but de las Carreras thinks that this might put too much pressure on Argentine supply.
"I have two hypotheses. According to the low end scenario, Argentina is exporting 640,000 tonnes a year by 2000. In the best case it is exporting 830,000 tonnes," he said.
Argentine domestic beef consumption is roughly stable at just under two million tonnes, with a gradual fall in per-capita demand compensated by population growth.
Gaining access to Japan and South Korea, which is vital for export growth, may not prove easy, added Martinez.
"The negotiations with the Japanese have been very complicated, despite the U.S. approval," she said, "They have not shown much enthusiasm."
